speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 wish to speak briefly on Bill C-54 with regard to the energy section, the effects of the budget, and the disastrous effect of the Liberal energy policy on the industry and the country as a whole. What is most disturbing is the attitude of the government, which has made it perfectly clear that it will keep us on this disastrous course. We are going to have to keep hammering away until we can get ministers to budge on the position they have taken.
1 want to congratulate the hon. member for Pembina on his remarks. He certainly made one point very clear-never trust a Liberal.
I should like to comment on some correspondence we have received from the oil industry and the drilling industry in Canada about the very serious and damaging effects the Liberal energy policy has on them. I want to quote from a letter dated January 26 this year from the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada to the Prime Minister. The letter points out:
After three months of careful study we the members of the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada have concluded that the National Energy Program (NEP) will have disastrous consequences not only for our industry but for Canada's national goal of energy self-sufficiency and, indeed, the over-all economy.
We represent the Canadian owned and controlled independent segment of the oil and gas industry in our country.
I want to emphasize that I am talking about Canadian companies, Mr. Chairman, not multinationals or oil barons. We are talking about small Canadian companies that are being harassed and chased out of the country by Liberal policies.
The letter goes on:
We have no quarrel with the stated objectives of the NEP. We simply do not believe the program will achieve them; moreover, it will prove to be counterproductive to those objectives.
Every document, letter, magazine or newspaper 1 picked up has this same phrase, "counterproductive to those objectives". So we are going backwards under their ridiculous policy.
The letter continues:
In view of the far-reaching national and international implications of the NEP. we respectfully request that your government establish a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons to undertake a full examination of the impact and ramifications of the National Energy Program.
Again referring to the National Energy Program, the letter goes on to point out:
These implications include the health of the national economy, jobs in every part of Canada, the secure supply of oil over the immediate and longer term, our international trade and baiance of payments, and the unity of the country. Indeed, as stated in the NEP itself, the program "will impinge... in almost every sphere of Canadian activity,-"
The activity seems to be taking place at the borders where trucks are lined up loaded with drilling equipment moving out of the country.
It was reported the other day that at Coutts, Alberta, there was a line-up of trucks of one mile long last week. The energy minister disputed this today, but we are getting pictures of
January 28, 1981

these trucks lined up and leaving. 1 am sure the minister would say that the picture in the Red Deer Advocate is false and that they are telling lies and that this is not happening. I doubt very much if the Advocate is publishing false pictures and giving false information about drilling equipment and trucks leaving Canada. A report in last Thursday's Advocate states as follows:
Rigs Leave-A convoy of trucks carrying a disassembled oil drilling rig clears through United States customs at Coutts on the Albcrta-Montana border Thursday. This rig, owned by Hi-Towcr Drilling Ltd. of Edmonton, needed 30 trucks to transport it, although some require up to 60 trucks. About 50 rigs have moved south through Coutts since last October when the federal energy policy was announced.
Today the hon. member for Assiniboia gave more figures about the devastating effect this is having on the province of Saskatchewan. The Saskoil Company is applying to do drilling in Montana. How are we to become self-sufficient when this sort of thing happens? I think the reason the Liberals are continuing with this disastrous policy is because they are trying to squirm out of the ridiculous statement they made in the last election campaign that they were going to get cheap gas for Canadians. 1 think they had better get off that "cheap gas" idea and tell the truth to the Canadian people. They should tell the people how much of their money is being spent daily to bring imported oil from the OPEC countries. I brought this up in a motion today, Mr. Chairman. It costs $12 million per day for oil from the OPEC countries. They will become wealthy and have all their people working. But not this country, Mr. Chairman.
I should now like to read part of a letter from the chairman of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited-not some company over in Africa or Asia. The letter states:
Since the passing of the October budget, and the introduction of the National Energy Program, parliamentary and media debate on Canadian energy policy has been intense. As chairman of one of Canada's principal petroleum companies, I am acutely aware of the importance, not only to the industry but also to the economic and social well-being of Canadians, of an energy policy of optimum benefit to the nation.
He enclosed a brochure. 1 shall not read all of it but just some of the more important parts. On page 5 it states:
The over-all impact of the measures proposed in the National Energy Program will be a very sharp decline in the industry's cash flows and earnings.
With double-digit inflation, Mr. Chairman, you need a large cash flow. You cannot work on a little bit of cash flow.
It continues:
All of the industry forecasts, as well as those made by other knowledgeable observers, indicate that the industry's cash flow will be reduced by approximately 30 per cent and its net earnings by about 50 per cent. This inevitably will result in a substantial reduction in exploration and development activity in western Canada. It also will seriously impair the industry's ability to undertake the risks and finance the massive investment required for development of the oil sands and the frontiers.
So much for energy self-sufficiency under this National Energy Program and these clauses of Bill C-54.
On page 6 the brochure states:
In short, we are firmly convinced that an arbitrarily defined requirement for Canadian control to qualify for the proposed Canadian ownership incentives is not only unnecessary but would unfairly penalize many Canadians who already
Income Tax Act
own shares in the industry. It also could discourage foreign-conlrollcd companies from making shares available for purchase by Canadian investors and thus prove counterproductive to the achievement of greater Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry.
Everything that this government has come out with since it got back into office is counterproductive. It has made absolutely no headway at all in any area.
I have a letter here from a small Canadian company which is struggling to survive, called Riley's Datashare International Ltd., based in Calgary. The letter which was sent to all members on our side of the House states:
Enclosed is an interim financial report which outlines our position on the National Energy Program.
Riley's Datashare International is a data service company providing products to the petroleum industry around the world from offices in Calgary and Houston. We arc a public company with over 1,300 shareholders, more than 90% of whom are Canadian residents. While a small company of just 200 employees, 140 of which arc in Canada, we believe we arc representative of the many petroleum service companies who will be hurt by the NEP.
It is all the little companies, the medium-sized companies and indeed even the multinationals that are being hurt-are getting walloped by these policies. Of course in the end we suffer too.
The letter concludes with the following:
In our view, the program is in need of drastic revision. It threatens economic activity, is furthering the sense of regionalism in western Canada, and jeopardizes our chances of energy security. We urgently suggest reassessment.
1 hope that in the near future the finance minister or the energy minister will come up with some way of reassessing or withdrawing this program. They cannot continue with this ridiculous procedure in light of all the evidence that is coming from these firms. We cannot assume they are all lying to us or giving us false information. If they are, then someone had better get up and discount it.
Riley's also enclosed a brochure. In part, under the heading of "National Energy Program" we read:
The major event of the second quarter without doubt was the federal government's National Energy Program and the continued inability of the two senior levels of government in Canada to reach an agreement on petroleum pricing and revenue sharing. Much coherent and sincere opposition to the NEP is being made by the petroleum industry in terms of the impact on the industry and the nation as a whole. In our view the inappropriateness of the program traces to several inconsistent objectives:
They go into great detail about how the program is affecting them. They comment on "Self-sufficiency-Activity" as follows:
The federal government remains committed to energy security and yet the net effect of the NEP is to reduce the industry's ability and willingness to achieve this. Industry cash flow under the program will be reduced.
They go on to explain how this program is affecting their firm and its expansion.
Neither the Minister of Finance nor the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is here, but the Minister of State for Finance is. 1 would like to refer to Oilweek magazine for January 12, 1981. There is a lengthy article quoting statements and comments made by various provincial cabinet min-

January 28, 1981
Income Tax Act
isters, as well as statements by people in the industry. The only favourable comments 1 can find in this magazine are some statements made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, but the other 15 or 20 statements are extremely critical of the National Energy Program. I think the minister would learn a lot about his government's programs and the effect they are having on the nation if he would read this magazine. If he has not, I would suggest that it would make great reading for him tonight.
The statement by Mr. Robert H. McClelland, minister of energy, mines and petroleum resources for the province of British Columbia, is headed "Significant Slump Expected". 1 will not read his statement in full, but in part it reads:
-unless the federal government seriously reconsiders its positions, the outlook is very discouraging.
Then there is considerable detail, similar to what was in the two letters I received this week.
The next article to which 1 will refer is by Mr. Selby W. Porter, president, Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors. This is not a multinational firm nor does it have anything to do with OPEC. He states:
The combination of the recent federal budget, the national energy program, the lack of a pricing agreement for crude oil between the federal government and the producing provinces, and the declining gas sales and exports to the United States, combine to ensure a downturn of exploratory and development activity in 1981.
How on earth can we become self-sufficient when every oil company and drilling company is winding down?
Mr. Porter goes on to say:
The outlook for 1981 in the present circumstances is dismal for the contracting industry; with a forecast of only 5,800 wells to be drilled in 1981, and as a consequence we arc faced with the prospect of a large surplus of equipment, service facilities and personnel.
This doom and gloom story goes on. Here is a statement by Mr. Jack M. MacLeod, chairman of the board of governors, Canadian Petroleum Association. The heading of his article is "Self sufficiency goal slips away". Here is another statement: "Canada's potential continues to be frustrated by the failures of our national policies."
I cannot find any statement anywhere which gives this government any credit at all for any of its energy or budget policies. I do not know whether this minister wants to make a statement today as to whether the government is looking at changes, is concerned, or whether this is all false information which these people are handing out.
If the minister would like to take a few minutes to make a statement as a start, we would certainly appreciate hearing from him. The explanation to date from the energy minister was meaningless. Perhaps this minister might have a better explanation as to what corrective measures the government is going to take.

I have a few questions for the minister and I hope he will take note of them this afternoon although, 1 do not know why he would have his officials here if he is not answering questions. My questions are not so much to do with what is in the bill but rather about matters which were left out of the bill. I would have hoped that those questions could have been answered, but I am prepared, if everyone else is, to wait until the minister sums up the discussions with respect to clause 1 of the bill.
At the outset, 1 want to make a few comments following on those of my colleagues who spoke earlier. The government should not be too surprised if, when dealing with a tax bill, we talk about such matters as energy, and the economic policy in general, and matters which strike even deeper to the very foundation of the institution as it will be affected in the future by the arrangements we are presently discussing with regard to constitutional reform.
I have here a document. It is a copy of a book in our library which the hon. member for Victoria dug up. It lays out the procedure one would follow to establish an extreme radical alternative to the type of western democracy on which our system is built. The book is called "Birth of the Communist Manifesto". The early advocates of communism talked about some of the things one would have to do in order to achieve a redistribution of wealth and the transfer of productive mechanisms away from the bourgeoisie to the workers. According to this book, the following would be required, and I quote:
Income Tax Act
!. Abolition of property in land and application of all rents of land to public purposes.
2.	A heavy progressive or graduated income tax.
3.	Abolition of all right of inheritance.
4.	Confiscation of the property of all emigrants and rebels.
5.	Centralization of credit in the hands of the State, by means of a national bank with State capital and an exclusive monopoly.
6.	Centralization of the means of communication and transport in the hands of the State.
7.	Extension of factories and instruments of production owned by the State; the bringing into cultivation of wastelands, and the improvement of the soil generally in accordance with a common plan.
8.	Equal liability of all to labour. Establishment of industrial armies, especially for agriculture.
It goes on and on. What struck me when reading this is that when you go over it you see that many of these things have already been achieved in our society. This document is the foundation for a very progressive and graduated income tax act. The imposition of those kinds of taxes on property would demean them in a way to affect their value when inherited by one's children.
We already have the centralization of banks. Of late, in our constitutional debate, we have been talking about the nationalization of property. It is being said that the right to own property will no longer be looked at as a right in the future, but rather as a privilege. The right to own property, which in my opinion is the most fundamental basis of western civilization, would no longer be respected in our constitution. I wish to quote another sentence from this very interesting document:
In this sense, the theory of the Communists may be summed up in the single sentence: Abolition of private property.
I do not suggest this government is about to go out and confiscate property. However, we do have that in our energy program. There is a clear confiscation of private assets in the sense that, if they are located on federal lands, the Crown corporation will be directed to move in and assume 25 per cent ownership in the lands and the improvements that have been made under the lease without compensation. If that is not confiscation, I would like someone more knowledgeable to explain what it is.
These people, together with their friends to my left, have done more than that. They are abolishing God. I was tempted to stand up before question period today and move a motion under Standing Order 43 suggesting that we rename this place Babylon, and rename our Prime Minister "the king of Babylon". Obviously he has anointed himself as God. He is wiser than the Almighty. We no longer need any reference to God in our constitution. I do not want to be unkind to the right hon. gentleman, but I sincerely hope that he will not be destined to suffer the same fate as the king of Babylon. As you know, when the king of Babylon denounced Jehovah, a mysterious fiery hand came out and wrote on the wall, "weighed, counted and divided". Of course he was assassinated the same night he made the pronouncement. I do not wish that our Prime Minister be assassinated, but I wish he would reassess in more realistic terms the effects of his type of a new society which he is perpetrating upon us.

Income Tax Act
After that rather gloomy opening, I want to address some remarks to the minister who previously showed some interest in a proposal I made with regard to northern benefits. This is more directly related to the bill. I wish the minister would make some notes and respond to my questions, either now or at an agreed time.
There is a reference in the bill regarding northern benefits. There is a remission order which allows certain northern benefits which employers in northern and remote areas of the country pay to their employees on which no income tax is payable. These benefits are now identified. They basically have to do with travel, housing subsidies, and other direct costs for which the employer wishes to compensate the employee. There is no remission at the moment for actual northern benefits paid out in cash.
I spoke yesterday in the Elouse with respect to my proposals. I laid out to hon. members, and specifically to the minister, the rather serious inequity which exists in northern Canada where living costs are much higher than in other parts of the country. I pointed out the effects of this kind of insensitive income tax policy on lower-income people in the north, particularly those on fixed incomes, old age pensions, unemployment insurance and other forms of social assistance. The payments are the same everywhere in this country. An unemployment cheque is the same amount for a person north of 60 as in the rest of the province. The amount of the old age pension is the same. However, living costs are three times higher in some areas than in the cities.
With the evidence produced through my report, we had every right to expect some reflection of the proposals, which are being actively studied by the department, in this bill. There is no doubt that the report is based on logic. The government compensates employees in the north with cash payments to mitigate the cost differences, the financial hardships associated with northern living. The federal government pays between $1,000 and $12,000 a year to employees of the public service who are posted in isolated areas. I would ask the minister whether it would not be reasonable to expect, if it is costly and difficult for federal employees or employees of large corporations, both of which have chosen to compensate their employees, to cope with these special circumstances, that it is equally costly and difficult for every other Canadian living in the north?
I have enumerated some of the problems that add to the cost of northern living, including the high cost of gasoline. I have pointed out some areas where a gallon of gasoline costs $5 or $6, and that perishable foods have to be flown in by aircraft and therefore are three or four times the cost in cities.
1 have pointed out that other countries with similar geographic difficulties are dealing with this problem by establishing different tax zones and allowing taxpayers in those zones greater personal exemptions in order to equalize opportunities and to achieve a greater degree of equality and fairness in the sense of income tax. After all, equity and fairness are supposed
to be the basis of the act. With a graduating and progressive tax scheme one is supposed to be charged taxes in accordance with his ability to pay, and there is no doubt that one's ability to pay in this country varies very dramatically in accordance with where one lives.
1 was able to table my report before the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. 1 know the minister of the department has a serious commitment to give earnest study to that document. I am also told that the committee on northern affairs, on finance, and national revenue, and the officials of the three departments are seriously looking at the whole question of northern benefits and will be making recommendations to the cabinet, the Treasury Board, and the Minister of National Revenue in relation to the handling of the tax act as it applies to northern residents.
1 notice that the Minister of National Revenue has just entered the chamber. I know as well of his interest. He has written to me and has said they are earnest and serious in their assessment of this rather serious situation. What I would ask him to do is nothing else but to use the same criteria the federal government uses to compensate its northern employees in terms of housing subsidies, cash payments or northern living allowances, applying that same criteria on a more universal basis, namely, to use the Income Tax Act to allow all northern residents, whether they work for the government, some other business or even northern businessmen, to make the same kind of deductions. After all, that must only be fair.
I would ask him to study seriously, for instance, what Australia is doing in that regard, and what Denmark is doing in its treatment of taxpayers in Greenland. These people undoubtedly have come to the same conlusion that I reached. I want to tell the minister how serious this matter is for the 5 per cent of Canadians who live in the two tax zones I have identified in my study. This percentage of people would have paid $470 million too much in personal income tax if nothing else were done except the application of these criteria. That has to be very dramatic. In many cases the tax dollar is taking food out of the mouths of children. Their parents cannot afford the kind of nutritious food other Canadians could not possibly do without.
1 would ask the minister to look seriously at that. I can assure him there is a wide community and constituency of support for this proposal. Certainly the federation of independent business people has embraced the proposal as a policy and many of the unions operating in the north, the steelworkers, for instance, have made that their national policy. Every municipality in the north has written me letters of support, and I am sure the minister has received letters as well. Strangely enough, as I speak on open line programs throughout the country I get nothing but a positive response, even from people in the larger cities who just simply do not understand how difficult and costly it is to cope with the harsh realities of northern winters, the isolation, and having to send children two or three thousand miles away to learning institutions, or to hospitals for special medical treatment, and so on.

All I am saying is that in order to achieve any degree of equity and fairness in the north, the Income Tax Act would be the tool to use. The establishment of different tax zones would be a method that is acceptable. It has been proven in many other countries and deserves the consideration of this government. I am very disappointed that some of these proposals were not reflected in this particular bill, but 1 am hopeful the minister, in response to my comments, will be able to enlighten us as to how the multidepartmental study is going and what the government's views are in respect of these proposals.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak for just a moment about the special 50 per cent investment tax credit proposed in this bill.
In my view the designation of areas to receive the special 50 per cent investment tax credit should involve regions of the country which suffer the effects of regional disparity, instead of census divisions within regions and, indeed, within provinces. Last Wednesday I spoke at length on this matter and made my argument in that regard. Today I should like to detail a few points in support of my argument.
According to the data base on which the program is based, 13 of the 42 areas selected do not qualify for designation with regard to the per capita income and family unemployment rate criteria used in the selection process. An additional factor, that of isolation, has to be included in order to effect the qualification.
Eleven areas that do not qualify under the per capita income and family unemployment rate criteria are not included. I would like to illustrate this point by referring to the census divisions identified in the province of Quebec.
L'Islet, census division 13, has a per capita income of $2,760 and a family unemployment rate of 3.3 per cent. This area is not included, while Riviere du Loup, census division 8, with a per capita income of $3,577 and a lower family unemployment rate of 3 per cent, is included.
L'Islet is part of Bellechasse, which for a long time was represented by a distinguished Social Credit member of Parliament, and is now represented by an able member of the government caucus, who may wish to pursue this matter. If he does so, the research material I have gathered will be available to him.
Labelle, census division 16, has a per capita income of $3,227 and a family unemployment rate of 3 per cent. Again, Labelle is worse off than Riviere du Loup, but it too is excluded, and 1 have to ask why.
Charlevoix, which is represented in the House by my friend, the Minister of State for Small Businesses, has a per capita income of $4,000 and a family unemployment rate of 3.2 per cent, but is not included as an area designated to receive the benefit. Apparently the Minister of State for Small Businesses does not enjoy the same good fortune as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and the Minister of Finance whose constituencies are included. That is quite understandable, but perhaps the Minister of State for Small Businesses will have some difficulty explaining to his constituents how the

Minister of National Revenue was so fortunate as to have part of his constituency included, with a per capita average income of $5,531 and a family unemployment rate of only 1.5 per cent, in census district number 10, which is Labrador.
I want to be the first one to suggest that the answer is to be found in the weight that is given to an isolation factor, but looking at the per capita income of $5,531 which is higher than most included areas of Quebec, and a family unemployment rate of 1.5 per cent-a lower unemployment rate than all the other areas in Quebec which are included-I have to suggest to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and the Minister of National Revenue that that is some isolation factor!

Part of Thunder Bay district, in census district 58 which is included, has an average income of $6,827 and a family unemployment rate of 2 per cent. Again, it must be some heavy weight that is given to the isolation factor!
If the isolation factor is great in Ontario, some other mysterious and powerful force is at work in Nova Scotia. The Minister of Finance must be delighted that Inverness, census district 15 in his riding, with an average per capita income of $3,674 and a family unemployment rate of 3.1 per cent, is included, while the member for South West Nova is hung out to dry in respect of Digby, census district number 3 in her riding, which has a per capita income of $2,826 and a family unemployment rate of 3.3 per cent. Mr. Chairman, like my colleagues, 1 have a terrible temptation to use clause 1 of this bill for a global assault on a government which richly deserves it, but in the interest of time I will zero right in on a point which 1 wish to draw to the attention of the Minister of State for Finance and also of the Minister of National Revenue who is here, because what 1 am going to talk about, Mr. Chairman, is the question of voluntary agencies in Canada and the income tax amendment which is very sorely needed on their behalf which will, at one and the same time, be a social advance in this country and save the government $93 million. A proposal to improve the social conditions in our country and make a substantial saving to the public taxpayer, to the government, is a proposal which, if you do not want to build a monument to the one who makes it, at least should be taken seriously by a government concerned about the public purse today.
It is not a new proposal, Mr. Chairman. 1 am bringing it up again in this debate because the government has not moved on the proposal which has been put forward in the form of various motions over the years by about half a dozen members, and most recently by myself on June 9, 1980. 1 draw to the minister's attention pages 1898 to 1905 of Hansard of that day. In that debate is to be found the detail of a proposal which is not terribly complicated but which contains many figures to sustain the point f made a moment ago, which is that my proposal would actually result in saving the government $93 million in the initial year.
In essence, the proposal is that the standard $100 deduction for charitable donations be done away with and that taxpayers be given an option of either claiming their gifts to charitable and voluntary organizations as deductions from taxable income, or be allowed to claim 50 per cent of the value of the gift or donation as a tax credit.
Doing away with the $100 standard deduction immediately saves the government, on the figures of 1977 which are the most recent ones available, $245 million. It also becomes much more fair to people who are actually giving donations to voluntary organizations, and it becomes more fair to the organizations because there is a greater incentive for people to make donations to voluntary organizations when they can be given the choice of a deduction, if their tax credit is such that it is more advantageous for them to do that, which it would be for high income earners, or the choice of claiming a tax credit for 50 per cent of the gift, which would apply to a great majority of income taxpayers in the middle to lower ends of the scale.
This is not a fly-by-night proposal. The origin of it goes back to the National Voluntary Organization, an umbrella group of 108 national voluntary and charitable organizations representing some 45,000 registered charities in Canada. These are organizations for the disadvantaged, the poor, the sick and the needy. They are organizations for children and the aged, health organizations, organizations for research into heart and lung disease, cancer, diabetes, muscular dystrophy, health services for the mentally and physically handicapped. They are religious organizations sustaining and preserving our spiritual values, international development organizations, educational organizations, environmental organizations, native, ethnic and cultural organizations. There is a wide group within our society which this organization represents. Indeed it would be hard to think of a Canadian who is not touched one way or another by the social benefits provided to our society by voluntary organizations.
What is happening to voluntary organizations today? They are being hit by the inflation factor in such a way that patterns are now established of a decline in giving because of the squeeze in which so many people find themselves and the transferring of that financial squeeze to those groups that have hitherto been the beneficiaries of a charity based upon a reasonable financial position which is now being eroded as a result of inflation.
I am not advancing an argument against controlling inflation. I am only recognizing the inevitability of continuing inflation and what it is doing to voluntary and charitable organizations which perform such a tremendous service to our country. Briefly, they are in a tax squeeze.
If a change were made to the Income Tax Act along the lines that I have mentioned, the situation would be improved. 1 must say that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gave support to my proposal. Of course he entered certain caveats. There were certain measures in my motion about which the hon. member had some reservations. I accept those reservations because I am not wedded to the precise detail of how the Income Tax Act should be amended in such a way as to give incentive to people to increase their donations to voluntary and charitable organizations. I am only speaking to the principle of it, that the time has come to make a change to the Income Tax Act which will be of benefit to voluntary organizations and will be an enrichment to the social fabric of the country. I can say that there is widespread support in the House for such a move.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance responded to my motion, but he did not even bother to listen to the arguments or to figure out the actual computations of the figures which I advanced on behalf of national voluntary organizations. He made a canned speech which was written beforehand. The figures included in my motion to my knowledge have not yet been disputed by the Department of Finance.
January 28, 1981

I will not argue about a few dollars one way or another. 1 am only advancing the position that the introduction of such an amendment would be not only socially beneficial, but it would be a saving to taxpayers. 1 advanced the argument that the cost to government for such a proposal would be $391 million, whereas at the present time it costs $484 million in tax revenues because of the way in which the present law is written. The parliamentary secretary said that we cannot afford it. I say that we can. I say there is a widespread public support in Canada for such a move and that the lime has come for us to advance it.
I have received mail from various voluntary organizations and national associations all over the country. I will refer to only a few to show the wide range of support for this proposal-the Canadian Mental Health Association, the National Council of YMCAs of Canada, the Canadian Heart Foundation, the National Indian Brotherhood, Grant MacEwan Community College in Edmonton, and the Canadian Jesuit Missions. That is only a handful of the organizations in Canada which support the proposal and would be among the beneficiaries.
Finally 1 come to an argument which I think has an overriding appeal. When we consider what needs to be done to help voluntary organizations which are of tremendous benefit to the country, when we consider the widespread support for an income tax amendment which would increase the incentive for Canadians to give to those organizations, and when we consider that it would be a fair tax return to the Canadian government and to Canadian taxpayers, all of that should carry the case. But, there is one final argument.
On behalf of the political parties of this country we put in place a few years ago an income tax amendment which allowed people to give to political parties and to receive a tax write-off of 75 per cent at the bottom line. I think there is an argument to be advanced for political parties because they also make a very important contribution to the total fabric of our society. As a result of that income tax amendment, the political parties are now able to raise money despite inflation. They are able to raise plenty of money for their needs.
1 am particularly directing my remarks to the Minister of National Revenue. If we can make such an amendment on behalf of political parties, I submit the time has come for us to apply the same principle of a tax credit of 50 per cent at the bottom line-I am only asking for 50 per cent of what is given to registered charities and national voluntary organizations. If we can do it for political organizations, I submit the time has come in the spirit of social justice for us to do it for voluntary organizations which are providing such a tremendous benefit to everyone in the country.

Well, just to start off, we have heard some discussion about the problems in the tax laws of Canada. I am not sure whether it is because they are written by lawyers, economists, or computer experts in a computer language with which not too many of us are familiar.
From watching television and from reading my daily and weekly newspapers, I know that the government spends hundreds-and I would presume hundreds of thousands-of dollars of taxpayers' money telling Canadian taxpayers how simple and easy it is to understand the tax system.
1 should like to refer to one clause in Bill C-54. If the minister's officials feel able, when I come close to the end of my time, I would gladly give them an opportunity to explain it. Clause 66.2(6) reads as follows:
Where a non-resident person is a member of a partnership that is deemed under Paragraph I 15(4)(b) to have disposed of a property described in Subsection 59(1.1), his share of any amount that would be an amount referred to in Clause (5)(b)(v)(A) or Subparagraph (5)(b)(vi) or (xi) in respect of the partnership for a taxation year of the partnership if section 96 were read without reference to Paragraph (l)(d) thereof shall, for the purposes of this act, be deemed to be an amount referred to in Clause (5)(b)(v)(A) or Subparagraph (5)(b)(iv) or (xi), as the case may be, in respect of the non-resident person for the taxation year of the non-resident person that is deemed under Paragraph I I5(4)(a) to have ended.
I know that sounds like a speech made by the Minister of Transport, or maybe the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board in the other place. To be fair, I think it is maybe a bit extreme. But I think it is an example of the problems that we, as members of Parliament, have in trying to understand the tax laws. It is an example of additional costs accruing to individuals in Canada in trying to meet the requirements of good Canadian citizenship, that is, of fulfilling their tax obligations.
In Bill C-54, and in the budget, a considerable amount of time was spent with respect to the National Energy Program and also with respect to something called COR, Canadian Ownership Rate. I question the ability of this document to say what oil company in Canada, what company, could be called Canadian. There have been discussions with respect to that question during question period. 1 have been trying to read up on the subject to the best of my ability. There are two companies which come to mind when considering this matter, Dome Petroleum, which is considered by everyone to be Canadian, and Home Oil. The ownership rate which applies to Dome Petroleum, according to the rules as Jack Gallagher and I interpret them, is a tremendously difficult matter. The company's 15,287 registered shareholders, under the COR rules, only bring the Canadian ownership rate up to 52 per cent. Dome requested that it be able to purchase an interest in a company, of which it owns 49 per cent, in order to bring up its Canadian content. That company is TransCanada Pipe Lines. Is Dome Petroleum a Canadian company or is it not? Bill C-54 is mute on that.

The other company I mentioned, Home Oil, is owned 100 per cent by Hiram-Walker Consumers Home Ltd. If the same rules are applied to Home Oil it is 75 per cent to 80 per cent Canadian-owned. These circumstances illustrate some of the problems which industry in Canada sees.
I would like to ask the Department of Finance if it is aware of the computer modules which the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has established, according to Edmund Clark, for the cash flow of every oil company in Canada? If the department is aware, does the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources accept the figures that the cash flow of the oil companies will be 28 per cent higher this year than last year, as stated by the Minister of Finance in answer to a question from the hon. member for Calgary Centre? This is cash flow which is needed by the oil companies for reinvestment. Or does the minister accept the figures of Mr. Bell, the Vice-President of Petro-Canada, which show that the cash flow of the oil companies will be 25 per cent less this year than they were last year?
If these computer modules are in place I do not see why there should be a discrepancy of over 50 per cent in these figures. Why is there this discrepancy between the figures of the Minister of Finance and the statement made yesterday in the Toronto Star by Mr. Bell?
I would also like to know if the department is aware that the figures for drilling for oil in Canada in the second quarter of 1981 will be 54 per cent to 58 per cent less than last year. If so, do the officials agree with those figures? Do they also agree that more than 50 per cent of the drilling rigs presently working will have their contracts expire before the second quarter of 1981? We hear the gobbledygook from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with respect to there being more rigs drilling this year that at the same time last year. If the minister were to take the time to visit western Canada and go into the oil-producing areas, he would hear some statistics which would bother him considerably.
Most of the drilling rigs are now under contract. The reason they are under contract is because until this present program was put in place under the National Energy Program the use of rigs was at a premium in Canada. So oil companies had to contract on a long-term basis in order to have rigs available. The rigs which are presently drilling are also drilling for another reason. We have heard figures about the increase in
drilling in Saskatchewan. The reason there was an increase in November and December is because of the credit system which was set up by the government of Saskatchewan. The system was such that if you drilled so many wells you would get an increase in your royalty. That system was removed as of January 1. So companies looked at their credit pool and decided that they must drill more wells in order to use up their credits. That is what they did. That is one of the reasons why there was more activity in the fourth quarter of 1979.
The problem we have in my constituency is with respect to capital gains. Several of my colleagues have spoken about this matter. In my opinion the capital gains tax is a tax after a tax. In view of statements made here I am sure everyone is aware of the promise made during the election campaign by the government. Ministers promised to change V-Day for capital gains from 1971 to 1974 values. I wonder if the minister could explain why this has not been done. Perhaps I have misread something because of my inability to read computereeze. I do not think I have. I think it is something which this government promised and which it has not given. It is like so many other things. What bothers me with respect to capital gains is that we in this party seem to be the only ones in this House who think it is a double tax.
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood accused the government of abandoning a field of wealth taxation when it removed the taxation on capital gains and estate taxes in 1972. We in this party do not stand for a death tax. Apparently the NDP does. I find it strange that the hon. member for Vancouver East suggested in this House that there should be a 100 per cent capital gains tax. The farmers in Saskatchewan, even the ones in NDP constituencies, do not believe there should be a 100 per cent capital gains tax on their sweat, blood and toil, on that which has taken them sometimes three or four generations to build up. This government made a commitment to remove some of the onerous aspects of the capital gains tax in its election promises in the February campaign. We look forward to seeing those promises kept when Bill C-54 is translated into English or French.
